en.title: 7 Books You Need to Discover This Month
en.summary: From award-winning authors to buzzy debuts, this curated list highlights essential reads across genres that are capturing attention right now.
en.body:
## 1. Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li
This historical fiction epic, penned by the award-winning Yiyun Li, transports readers to late 18th-century Dublin, Russia, and India. It masterfully explores the lives of ambitious artists, centering on the gifted pianist Adelaide Percheron and her future husband, John Field, the very inventor of the term "nocturne." It's a deep dive into artistic passion and historical settings.

## 2. The Occidental Book of the Dead by T. Geronimo Johnson
Prepare for a potent, immersive experience with T. Geronimo Johnson's latest. Following his critically acclaimed *Welcome to Braggsville*, this novel promises a profound exploration of identity and societal pressures. It centers on a Black cop whose life of assimilation is shattered by a violent confrontation with a white teen, forcing a reckoning with his past and present.

## 3. The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford by Nafissa Thompson-Spires
Nafissa Thompson-Spires, known for her sharp insights, delivers a compelling narrative that delves into complex relationships and untold stories. This book is a must-read for its intricate character studies and exploration of hidden histories, offering a unique perspective on domestic dynamics.

## 4. Vigil by George Saunders
George Saunders, a master of the short form, brings his signature blend of empathy and dark humor to this novel. *Vigil* is already generating significant buzz for its exploration of identity and retribution. The story follows Jackson, a mixed-race massage therapist, and three other queer men who team up to uncover who is targeting them, using their perceived sameness to their advantage.

## 5. Transcription by Ben Lerner
Ben Lerner's latest, *Transcription*, is a slender yet impactful novella that has quickly become a talking point. Described as "formally unstable" by The New Yorker, it challenges conventional narrative structures. This book is for readers who appreciate experimental storytelling and thought-provoking literary explorations.

## 6. The MASH Up by Laurie Marie Meyers
Laurie Marie Meyers introduces a fresh voice with *The MASH Up*, a title that promises an engaging and potentially genre-bending narrative. While details are scarce, its inclusion on radar lists suggests a unique premise and a story that stands out in the crowded literary landscape of July 2026.

## 7. Land: A Novel by Maggie O'Farrell
Maggie O'Farrell, a celebrated author, offers *Land*, a novel that is sure to be a significant literary event. Known for her evocative prose and compelling character development, O'Farrell's latest is a highly anticipated addition to any reader's list, hinting at a story rich in emotional depth and historical resonance.
Bottom Line: This month's must-reads offer a compelling mix of literary ambition, genre exploration, and timely themes.

content_raw: With the start of October, there’s been round-up after round-up of the most anticipated and best books coming out this month. Since fall has only just begun, these lists—which are conveniently gathered here —have banger after banger. I’ve parsed through them to bring you a sampling of the BIPOC releases that our staff is also excited about. There’s historical fantasy that imagines the lives of real musicians (who end up married), a trifling moonshiner’s murder (it’s award-nominated), historical romantasy based on the last Incan emperor, and more. And, just as a reminder since these books technically came out at the end of September, there’s Mazywood by Tananarive Due and The True Confessions of First Lady Freeman by Deesha Philyaw to also add to your list. Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li The award-winning Li’s latest is historical fiction that sweeps across late 18th-century Dublin, England, Russia, and India as it explores the story of the talented pianist Adelaide Percheron and her future husband, John Field (who invented the term “nocturne”), and their lives as ambitious artists. —Erica Ezeifedi The Occidental Book of the Dead by T. Geronimo Johnson This is the thickest book on my TBR so far. PEN/Faulkner Finalist T. Geronimo Johnson’s previous novel, Welcome to Braggsville , got a lot of love in addition to being longlisted for the National Book Award. I’m readying myself for a deep, potent read with this book about a Black cop shaken out of his life of assimilation after a confrontation with a white teen turns violent. —S. Zainab Williams The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford by Nafissa Thompson-Spires Thompson-Spires’ short story collection was longlisted for the National Book Award, and now her debut novel is shortlisted for the First Novel Prize . And it’s messy . In it, the trifling Rich Milford is dead, but I wouldn’t say anyone is really and truly sad about it, seeing as he was a no-good, womanizing moonshiner. But there still is the question of who exactly killed him in this Great Depression-era literary mystery. —Erica Ezeifedi The Savage Mind: An American Legacy by David Treuer With The Savage Mind , Treuer joins the tradition writers like James Baldwin and Ta-Nehisi Coates have taken part in by writing of this country’s ills in letter format. He merges both the personal and historical to explore the white settler violence that happened at the “frontier,” and how it is still perpetuated today. —Erica Ezeifedi The Lost Guardian by Natalia Hernandez This modern-day historical romantasy is based on the true history of Atahualpa, the last emperor of the Inca people.
